Project 1: Time-dependent evolution of a Gaussian wavepacket in 1D

Part (a): Numerical Method

Split operator

In physical units

For a lot of systems, V(x,t)=V(x)V(x,t) = V(x)V(x,t)=V(x). Using that, the hamiltonian operator operates entirely in the realm of position. For these systems, we have ψt=e−itH^/ℏψ0\psi_t = e^{-it\hat H/\hbar}\psi_0ψt​=e−itH^/ℏψ0​ . This is again similar to what we got for classical Hamiltonian systems. The full derivation for this is attached in my Notes.

Take a look at this equation :

eit2H^/ℏψt=ψt/2=e−it2H^/ℏψ0e^{i\frac{t}{2}\hat H/\hbar}\psi_t = \psi_{t/2}= e^{-i\frac{t}{2}\hat H/\hbar}\psi_0 ei2t​H^/ℏψt​=ψt/2​=e−i2t​H^/ℏψ0​

We can approximate this for small ttt as :

(1+it2H^/ℏ)ψt≈(1−it2H^/ℏ)ψ0(1+i\frac{t}{2}\hat H/\hbar)\psi_t \approx (1 - i\frac{t}{2}\hat H/\hbar)\psi_0 (1+i2t​H^/ℏ)ψt​≈(1−i2t​H^/ℏ)ψ0​

Then, for small Δx\Delta xΔx, we can discretise the ∂2∂x2\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}∂x2∂2​ operation and write :

ψt(x+Δx)+(4mΔx2tℏi−2mΔx2ℏ2V(x)−2)ψt(x)+ψt(x−Δx)≈−ψ0(x+Δx)+(4mΔx2tℏi+2mΔx2ℏ2V(x)+2)ψ0(x)−ψ0(x−Δx)\psi_t(x+\Delta x) + (\frac{4m\Delta x^2}{t\hbar}i - \frac{2m\Delta x^2}{\hbar^2}V(x) -2)\psi_t(x) + \psi_t(x-\Delta x) \\ \approx \\ - \psi_0(x+\Delta x) + (\frac{4m\Delta x^2}{t\hbar}i + \frac{2m\Delta x^2}{\hbar^2}V(x) + 2)\psi_0(x) - \psi_0(x-\Delta x) ψt​(x+Δx)+(tℏ4mΔx2​i−ℏ22mΔx2​V(x)−2)ψt​(x)+ψt​(x−Δx)≈−ψ0​(x+Δx)+(tℏ4mΔx2​i+ℏ22mΔx2​V(x)+2)ψ0​(x)−ψ0​(x−Δx)

Define

a(x)=4mΔx2tℏi−2mΔx2ℏ2V(x)−2b(x)=4mΔx2tℏi+2mΔx2ℏ2V(x)+2a(x) = \frac{4m\Delta x^2}{t\hbar}i - \frac{2m\Delta x^2}{\hbar^2}V(x) -2 \\ b(x) = \frac{4m\Delta x^2}{t\hbar}i + \frac{2m\Delta x^2}{\hbar^2}V(x) + 2 a(x)=tℏ4mΔx2​i−ℏ22mΔx2​V(x)−2b(x)=tℏ4mΔx2​i+ℏ22mΔx2​V(x)+2

Then, we can write :

[1a(x)1][ψt(x+Δx)ψt(x)ψt(x−Δx)]=[−1b(x)−1][ψ0(x+Δx)ψ0(x)ψ0(x−Δx)]\begin{bmatrix}1 & a(x) & 1\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\psi_t(x+\Delta x) \\ \psi_t(x) \\ \psi_t(x-\Delta x)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & b(x) & -1\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\psi_0(x+\Delta x) \\ \psi_0(x) \\ \psi_0(x-\Delta x)\end{bmatrix} [1​a(x)​1​]​ψt​(x+Δx)ψt​(x)ψt​(x−Δx)​​=[−1​b(x)​−1​]​ψ0​(x+Δx)ψ0​(x)ψ0​(x−Δx)​​

From here, you can write the equation for the whole grid/segment using tridiagonal matrices A,BA,BA,B as :

Aψ⃗t=Bψ⃗0A \vec \psi_t = B \vec \psi_0 Aψ​t​=Bψ​0​

And then solve this using tridiagonal matrix solvers from scipy that can solve this in O(N)O(N)O(N).

Atomic Units

For a single electron in first shell of hydrogen atom, we define:

α=14πϵ0qe2ℏc≈1137 andV1=qe24πϵ0a0=ℏ2meV1=4πϵ0ℏ2meqe2=ℏαmec=0.529×10−10 mE0=−V0=V1a0=qe4me(4πϵ0)2ℏ2=α2mec2=27.2eV\alpha = \frac{1}{4\pi \epsilon_0}\frac{q_e^2}{\hbar c} \approx \frac{1}{137}\quad \text{ and} \quad V_1 = \frac{q_e^2}{4\pi \epsilon_0}\\ a_0 = \frac{\hbar^2}{m_eV_1}= \frac{4\pi \epsilon_0 \hbar^2}{m_e q_e^2} = \frac{\hbar}{\alpha m_e c} = 0.529\times 10^{-10} \text{ m} \\ E_0 = -V_0 = \frac{V_1}{a_0}= \frac{q_e^4 m_e}{(4\pi\epsilon_0)^2 \hbar^2} = \alpha^2m_ec^2 = 27.2 \text{eV} α=4πϵ0​1​ℏcqe2​​≈1371​ andV1​=4πϵ0​qe2​​a0​=me​V1​ℏ2​=me​qe2​4πϵ0​ℏ2​=αme​cℏ​=0.529×10−10 mE0​=−V0​=a0​V1​​=(4πϵ0​)2ℏ2qe4​me​​=α2me​c2=27.2eV

With these constants, we make these substitutions in the TDSE :

x=x~a0V=V~E0t=t~ℏ/E0x = \tilde x a_0 \\ V = \tilde V E_0 \\ t = \tilde t \hbar/E_0 x=x~a0​V=V~E0​t=t~ℏ/E0​

This gives us the A-dimensional Time Dependent Schrodinger Equation (ATDSE) :

−12∂2ψ∂x~2+V~ψ=H~ψ=i∂ψ∂t~\boxed{ -\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial \tilde x^2} + \tilde V \psi = \tilde H \psi = i \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial \tilde t} } −21​∂x~2∂2ψ​+V~ψ=H~ψ=i∂t~∂ψ​​

Here H~=1E0H^=−12∂2∂x~2+V~\tilde H = \frac{1}{E_0} \hat H = -\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \tilde x^2} + \tilde VH~=E0​1​H^=−21​∂x~2∂2​+V~

Once again, assuming V~(x~,t~)=V~(x~)\tilde V(\tilde x,\tilde t) = \tilde V(\tilde x)V~(x~,t~)=V~(x~), we can write :

ψt=eiH^t/ℏψ0=eiH~t~ψ0\psi_t = e^{i\hat H t/\hbar}\psi_0 = e^{i \tilde H \tilde t }\psi_0 ψt​=eiH^t/ℏψ0​=eiH~t~ψ0​

The split operator approximation was:

ψt(x+Δx)+(4mΔx2tℏi−2mΔx2ℏ2V(x)−2)ψt(x)+ψt(x−Δx)≈−ψ0(x+Δx)+(4mΔx2tℏi+2mΔx2ℏ2V(x)+2)ψ0(x)−ψ0(x−Δx)\psi_t(x+\Delta x) + (\frac{4m\Delta x^2}{t\hbar}i - \frac{2m\Delta x^2}{\hbar^2}V(x) -2)\psi_t(x) + \psi_t(x-\Delta x) \\ \approx \\ - \psi_0(x+\Delta x) + (\frac{4m\Delta x^2}{t\hbar}i + \frac{2m\Delta x^2}{\hbar^2}V(x) + 2)\psi_0(x) - \psi_0(x-\Delta x) ψt​(x+Δx)+(tℏ4mΔx2​i−ℏ22mΔx2​V(x)−2)ψt​(x)+ψt​(x−Δx)≈−ψ0​(x+Δx)+(tℏ4mΔx2​i+ℏ22mΔx2​V(x)+2)ψ0​(x)−ψ0​(x−Δx)

This now becomes:

ψt~(x~+Δx~)+(4Δx~2t~i−2Δx~2V~(x~)−2)ψt~(x~)+ψt~(x~−Δx~)≈−ψ0(x~+Δx~)+(4Δx~2t~i+2Δx~2V~(x~)+2)ψ0(x~)−ψ0(x~−Δx~)\psi_{\tilde t}(\tilde x+\Delta \tilde x) + (\frac{4\Delta \tilde x^2}{\tilde t}i - 2\Delta \tilde x^2 \tilde V(\tilde x) -2)\psi_{\tilde t}(\tilde x) + \psi_{\tilde t}(\tilde x-\Delta \tilde x) \\ \approx \\ - \psi_0(\tilde x+\Delta \tilde x) + (\frac{4\Delta \tilde x^2}{\tilde t}i + 2\Delta \tilde x^2 \tilde V(\tilde x) + 2)\psi_0(\tilde x) - \psi_0(\tilde x-\Delta \tilde x) ψt~​(x~+Δx~)+(t~4Δx~2​i−2Δx~2V~(x~)−2)ψt~​(x~)+ψt~​(x~−Δx~)≈−ψ0​(x~+Δx~)+(t~4Δx~2​i+2Δx~2V~(x~)+2)ψ0​(x~)−ψ0​(x~−Δx~)

Similarly for the actual numerical method, now we define

a(x)=4Δx~2t~i−2Δx~2V~(x~)−2b(x)=4Δx~2t~i+2Δx~2V~(x~)+2a(x) = \frac{4\Delta \tilde x^2}{\tilde t}i - 2\Delta \tilde x^2\tilde V(\tilde x) -2 \\ b(x) = \frac{4\Delta \tilde x^2}{\tilde t}i + 2\Delta \tilde x^2\tilde V(\tilde x) + 2 a(x)=t~4Δx~2​i−2Δx~2V~(x~)−2b(x)=t~4Δx~2​i+2Δx~2V~(x~)+2

Using that, we write :

[1a(x~)1][ψt(x~+Δx~)ψt~(x~)ψt~(x~−Δx~)]=[−1b(x~)−1][ψ0(x~+Δx~)ψ0(x~)ψ0(x~−Δx~)]\begin{bmatrix}1 & a(\tilde x) & 1\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\psi_t(\tilde x+\Delta \tilde x) \\ \psi_{\tilde t}(\tilde x) \\ \psi_{\tilde t}(\tilde x-\Delta \tilde x)\end{bmatrix} \\ = \\ \begin{bmatrix}-1 & b(\tilde x) & -1\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\psi_0(\tilde x+\Delta \tilde x) \\ \psi_0(\tilde x) \\ \psi_0(\tilde x-\Delta \tilde x)\end{bmatrix} [1​a(x~)​1​]​ψt​(x~+Δx~)ψt~​(x~)ψt~​(x~−Δx~)​​=[−1​b(x~)​−1​]​ψ0​(x~+Δx~)ψ0​(x~)ψ0​(x~−Δx~)​​

Using this, tri-diagonal matrices A,BA,BA,B will be created, allowing us to do the implicit split-operator step by solving Aψt~=Bψ0A\psi_{\tilde t} = B \psi_0Aψt~​=Bψ0​ in O(N)O(N)O(N) operations using scipy.

For further accuracy, we can even go to a penta-diagonal matrix, using 5-point evaluation of the ∂2∂x2\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}∂x2∂2​ operator.

Space-Discretised Leap-Frog (SDLF)

The ATDSE is :

−12∂2∂x~2ψ+V~ψ=H~ψ=i∂∂t~ψ- \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \tilde x^2} \psi + \tilde V \psi= \tilde H \psi = i\frac{\partial }{\partial \tilde t}\psi −21​∂x~2∂2​ψ+V~ψ=H~ψ=i∂t~∂​ψ

Since the H~\tilde HH~ operator can be decomposed lineraly and maps real numbers to real numbers, we can write (after dropping the tilde) :

ψ=R+iI  ⟹  HR+iHI=i∂∂tR−∂∂tI  ⟹  ∂∂tI=HRand∂∂tR=−HI\psi = R + iI \implies \\ H R + i H I= i \frac{\partial }{\partial t} R - \frac{\partial }{\partial t} I \implies \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial t} I = H R \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial}{\partial t} R = - H I ψ=R+iI⟹HR+iHI=i∂t∂​R−∂t∂​I⟹∂t∂​I=HRand∂t∂​R=−HI

On top of this, we have

∫(I2+R2)dx=1\int (I^2 + R^2) dx = 1 ∫(I2+R2)dx=1

When descritised, this equation becomes

∑x(Ix2+Rx2)=1\sum_x (I_x^2 + R_x^2) = 1 x∑​(Ix2​+Rx2​)=1

Similarly, the evolution equations are discretised in space as :

∂∂tI[x]=V[x]R[x]−121Δx2(R[x+Δx]−2R[x]+R[x−Δx])∂∂tR[x]=−V[x]I[x]+121Δx2(I[x+Δx]−2I[x]+I[x−Δx])\frac{\partial}{\partial t} I[x] = V[x]R[x] - \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\Delta x^2} (R[x+\Delta x]-2R[x]+R[x-\Delta x]) \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial t} R[x] = -V[x]I[x] + \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\Delta x^2} (I[x+\Delta x]-2I[x]+I[x-\Delta x]) ∂t∂​I[x]=V[x]R[x]−21​Δx21​(R[x+Δx]−2R[x]+R[x−Δx])∂t∂​R[x]=−V[x]I[x]+21​Δx21​(I[x+Δx]−2I[x]+I[x−Δx])

We can rewrite the first equation as :

∂∂tI[x]=−12Δx2[1−2(1+V[x]Δx2)1][R[x+Δx]R[x]R[x−Δx]]\frac{\partial}{\partial t} I[x] = - \frac{1}{2\Delta x^2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2(1 + V[x]\Delta x^2) & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} R[x+\Delta x] \\ R[x] \\ R[x-\Delta x] \end{bmatrix} ∂t∂​I[x]=−2Δx21​[1​−2(1+V[x]Δx2)​1​]​R[x+Δx]R[x]R[x−Δx]​​

Define f[x]=−2(1+V[x]Δx2)f[x] = -2(1+V[x]\Delta x^2)f[x]=−2(1+V[x]Δx2) and then the tri-diagonal matrix

F=12Δx2[f[xl]100…001f[xl+Δx]10…0001f[xl+2Δx]1…00⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮0000…1f[xr]]F = \frac{1}{2\Delta x^2}\begin{bmatrix} f[x_l] & 1 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & f[x_l + \Delta x] & 1 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & f[x_l + 2\Delta x] & 1 & \dots & 0 & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 1 & f[x_r] \end{bmatrix} F=2Δx21​​f[xl​]10⋮0​1f[xl​+Δx]1⋮0​01f[xl​+2Δx]⋮0​001⋮0​…………​000⋮1​000⋮f[xr​]​​

Now, vectorising this, with R⃗=[Rx]x\vec R = [R_x]_xR=[Rx​]x​ and I⃗=[Ix]x\vec I = [I_x]_xI=[Ix​]x​, we can write :

∂∂tR⃗=FI⃗∂∂tI⃗=−FR⃗∣∣R⃗∣∣2+∣∣I⃗∣∣2=1\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\vec R = F \vec I\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\vec I = - F \vec R \\ ||\vec R||^2 + ||\vec I||^2 = 1 ∂t∂​R=FI∂t∂​I=−FR∣∣R∣∣2+∣∣I∣∣2=1

This is exactly how the hamiltonian systems we have seen evolve. The third equation is similar to the net energy being constant in a classical mechanics system.

So, just like before, we can use the position verlet LF integrator like so (for small step of size ttt):

R⃗t/2:=R⃗0+t2FI⃗0I⃗t:=I⃗0−tFR⃗t/2R⃗t:=R⃗t/2+t2FR⃗t/2\vec R_{t/2} := \vec R_0 + \frac{t}{2} F \vec I_0 \\ \vec I_{t} := \vec I_0 - t F \vec R_{t/2} \\ \vec R_t := \vec R_{t/2} + \frac{t}{2} F\vec R_{t/2} Rt/2​:=R0​+2t​FI0​It​:=I0​−tFRt/2​Rt​:=Rt/2​+2t​FRt/2​

Part (b): Normalization and Free Evolution

A gaussion packet with σ=0.7\sigma=0.7σ=0.7 centered at x0=−3x_0=-3x0​=−3 was initialised and given the average initial momentum/wave-number of k0=2k_0=2k0​=2. This was then evolved with a free potential. The evolution is visualised in the GIF animation shown. As you can see, the packet spreads in position-space as time passes, but doesn't spread in the wave-number/momentum domain. Here ϕ(k)\phi(k)ϕ(k) is computed using FFT. The derivations and exact method can be found in my Notes.

To verify that the normalisation actually happens, a plot of Nx(t)=⟨ψ∣ψ⟩N_x(t) = \braket{\psi|\psi}Nx​(t)=⟨ψ∣ψ⟩ is shown in the (static) figure, along with the normalisation NkN_kNk​ in the momentum domain. You can see that the variation for both NxN_xNx​ and NkN_kNk​ is on the order of 10−710^{-7}10−7.

It can in-fact be proven analytically that the SDLF method preserves the discreate analogues of the NxN_xNx​ and NkN_kNk​ values. For the derivation, see the section "Leap-Frog like finite difference method" in my Notes.

Part (c): Harmonic Oscillator (k0=0k_0 = 0k0​=0)

A gaussian packet with σ=0.7\sigma=0.7σ=0.7 was initialised at x0=−3x_0=-3x0​=−3 and was given no average momentum, i.e. k0=0k_0=0k0​=0. This was then evolved with the harmonic potential V0=12x2V_0=\frac{1}{2}x^2V0​=21​x2. You can see the periodic nature of the solution from the animation. Notice that here, the waveform in momentum space is also changing. This is because, unlike the free potential, with 0 classical force on the particle, here the classical force is F(x)=−ddxV=−2xF(x) = -\frac{d}{dx}V = -2xF(x)=−dxd​V=−2x. You can also see vertical lines for

  1. The most probable position xp(t)x_p(t)xp​(t) where ∣ψ(x,t)∣2|\psi(x,t)|^2∣ψ(x,t)∣2 is highest
  2. The mean position ⟨x⟩(t)\braket{x}(t)⟨x⟩(t), interpreting ∣ψ∣2(x,t)|\psi|^2(x,t)∣ψ∣2(x,t) as the probability density function.
  3. The classical solution xc(t)x_c(t)xc​(t) computed using (normal) Position-Verlet Leap-Frong integrator.

The same 3 quantities are also plotted as a function of time in a subplot of the static figure.

Part (d): Harmonic Oscillator (k0=2k_0 = 2k0​=2)

Now, the wave-packet is given an initial momentum of k0=2k_0=2k0​=2 rather than 0. This allows it to reach further to the right, as evident from the static plot for ⟨x⟩\braket{x}⟨x⟩; similar to how xcx_cxc​ goes further to the right than before. You will also notice that the average energy, namely ⟨H⟩(t)\braket{H}(t)⟨H⟩(t) is higher (see static figure) than what it was in the case when initial momentum was 0

Part (e): Numerical Stability and Accuracy

Chapter 8 for Wang's textbook says that the SDLF integrator will give stable solutions when Δt<λΔx2\Delta t < \lambda \Delta x^2Δt<λΔx2 where λ\lambdaλ is a characteristic of the potential V(x)V(x)V(x). It states that for a free potential, we have λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 and that for most potentials, λ=0.5\lambda=0.5λ=0.5 suffices. In the figure, I have plotted the trajectories for position, momentum, and the variation of Nx,NkN_x,N_kNx​,Nk​ and ⟨H⟩\braket{H}⟨H⟩ with time for various Δx,Δt\Delta x, \Delta tΔx,Δt as well as for the two methods discusses.
I initialised the wave-function as a gaussion with σ=0.7\sigma=0.7σ=0.7, centered at x0=−3x_0 = -3x0​=−3 and with initial average momentum of k0=0k_0 =0k0​=0. Then I evolved the packet using the harmonic potential V(x)=x2/2V(x)=x^2/2V(x)=x2/2.

You can see that for the cases when Δx=0.5\Delta x=0.5Δx=0.5, we get slight deviations of ⟨x⟩\braket{x}⟨x⟩ from the classical solution xcx_cxc​. This is expected, since the accuracy decreases on increasing Δx\Delta xΔx. You can also notice that the normalisation in position space, namely Nx(t)=⟨ψ∣ψ⟩N_x(t)=\braket{\psi|\psi}Nx​(t)=⟨ψ∣ψ⟩ suddenly increases by a significant amount for the case with Δx=0.1\Delta x=0.1Δx=0.1 and Δt=0.00825\Delta t=0.00825Δt=0.00825 when using the SDLF method. If I ran the simulation for a little longer, the numerical solution with these settings would become unstable and deviate by large amounts away from the classical solution. If you look closely, you can already see the start of this instability in the curve for ⟨x⟩\braket{x}⟨x⟩. This is because we don't have Δt<λΔx2\Delta t < \lambda \Delta x^2Δt<λΔx2 in this case. The split-operator method on the other hand, doesn't face this issue and performs well even when Δt\Delta tΔt is 0.05 (and Δx=0.1\Delta x =0.1Δx=0.1). Other than that, you will notice that the SDLF solution with Δx=0.1\Delta x=0.1Δx=0.1 is the closer to xcx_cxc​ and pcp_cpc​ curves than the split-operator solution, simply because it has a smaller Δt\Delta tΔt (though not small enough for numerical stability). Thus, just like always, a smaller Δt\Delta tΔt increases accuracy. Since these methods are 2nd order, the error scales as O(Δt2)O(\Delta t^2)O(Δt2).

Part (f): Linear Potential

I initialised the wave-packet with the same initial position and spread as all other parts, and 0 initial momentum. Then, I let it evolve under V(x)=Fx=xV(x)=Fx =xV(x)=Fx=x for a longer duration so that it hits the boundary. This was done intentionally to observe the effects of the boundary.

Since we assumed ψ=0\psi =0ψ=0 at the boundary at all times, we have effectively assumed that V=∞V=\inftyV=∞ outside the grid/segment we are solving for. This makes the boundaries perfectly reflective, with no part of the wavefunction being transmitted forward, and all probability mass reflected backwards. So, a wave moving towards left is reflected back. This reflected wave then interferes with the part of the original wave that is not yet reflected, giving us a wavy interference pattern. This can be seen towards the end of the animation.

Before the particle gets close to the boundary, it has constant acceleration and thus follows the equation ⟨x⟩≈xc=−3−12Ft2=−3−t2/2\braket{x} \approx x_c = -3 -\frac{1}{2}Ft^2 = -3 -t^2/2⟨x⟩≈xc​=−3−21​Ft2=−3−t2/2. This is a downward facing parabola, as evident from the subplot for position in the static figure. Note that even now, there is some effect from the boundary, but it isn't large enough for it to be visible. Another thing to note is that the average momentum also changes linearly, similar to the the classical solution. The wave-packet also spreads in position with time (see GIF animation), similar to what we saw in the case for the free particle.

Project 2: Radial Schrodinger equation for the hydrogen atom

Part (a): Effective Potential

Consider the 3D ATDSE with a central attractive potential V(r)V(r)V(r) where r=∣r∣r = |r|r=∣r∣:

−12∇2ψ(r⃗,t)+V(r)ψ(r⃗,t)=i∂∂tψ(r⃗,t)-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^2\psi(\vec r, t) + V(r)\psi(\vec r,t) = i\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\psi(\vec r, t) −21​∇2ψ(r,t)+V(r)ψ(r,t)=i∂t∂​ψ(r,t)

We can, as always, convert this to a time-independent equation as :

−12∇2ψ(r⃗)+V(r)ψ(r⃗)=Eψ(r⃗)-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^2\psi(\vec r) + V(r)\psi(\vec r) = E\psi(\vec r) −21​∇2ψ(r)+V(r)ψ(r)=Eψ(r)

Now, futher doing a separation of variables as ψ(r⃗)=R(r)Y(α,β)\psi(\vec r) = R(r)Y(\alpha, \beta)ψ(r)=R(r)Y(α,β) (where α\alphaα is the angle from the z axes and β\betaβ is the polar angle in the x-y plane) and using the spherical coordinate version of the laplacian, i.e.

∇2=1r2∂∂rr2∂∂r+1r21sin⁡α∂∂αsin⁡α∂∂α+1r21sin⁡2α∂2∂β2\nabla^2 = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r} r^2 \frac{\partial}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{1}{\sin \alpha}\frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \sin \alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} + \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{1}{\sin^2 \alpha}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta^2} ∇2=r21​∂r∂​r2∂r∂​+r21​sinα1​∂α∂​sinα∂α∂​+r21​sin2α1​∂β2∂2​

we can write :

∇2ψ(r⃗)=[1r2∂∂rr2∂∂rR]Y+[1r2R][1sin⁡α∂∂αsin⁡α∂∂αY+1sin⁡2α∂2∂β2Y]=2(V(r)−E)RY\nabla^2 \psi(\vec r) = [\frac{1}{r^2} \frac{\partial }{\partial r} r^2 \frac{\partial}{\partial r} R]Y + [\frac{1}{r^2}R][\frac{1}{\sin \alpha}\frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \sin \alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} Y + \frac{1}{\sin^2 \alpha}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta^2} Y] = 2(V(r)-E)RY ∇2ψ(r)=[r21​∂r∂​r2∂r∂​R]Y+[r21​R][sinα1​∂α∂​sinα∂α∂​Y+sin2α1​∂β2∂2​Y]=2(V(r)−E)RY

For the cases where ψ≠0,r≠0\psi \ne 0, r \ne 0ψ=0,r=0, we can write :

[1R∂∂rr2∂∂rR]+[1Y1sin⁡α∂∂αsin⁡α∂∂αY+1Y1sin⁡2α∂2∂β2Y]=2r2(V(r)−E)  ⟹  1Y1sin⁡α∂∂αsin⁡α∂∂αY+1Y1sin⁡2α∂2∂β2Y=2r2(V(r)−E)−1R∂∂rr2∂∂rR[\frac{1}{R} \frac{\partial }{\partial r} r^2 \frac{\partial}{\partial r} R] + [\frac{1}{Y}\frac{1}{\sin \alpha}\frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \sin \alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} Y + \frac{1}{Y}\frac{1}{\sin^2 \alpha}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta^2} Y] = 2r^2(V(r)-E) \\ \implies \\ \frac{1}{Y}\frac{1}{\sin \alpha}\frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \sin \alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} Y + \frac{1}{Y}\frac{1}{\sin^2 \alpha}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta^2} Y = 2r^2(V(r)-E) - \frac{1}{R} \frac{\partial }{\partial r} r^2 \frac{\partial}{\partial r} R [R1​∂r∂​r2∂r∂​R]+[Y1​sinα1​∂α∂​sinα∂α∂​Y+Y1​sin2α1​∂β2∂2​Y]=2r2(V(r)−E)⟹Y1​sinα1​∂α∂​sinα∂α∂​Y+Y1​sin2α1​∂β2∂2​Y=2r2(V(r)−E)−R1​∂r∂​r2∂r∂​R

Clearly, since LHS and RHS are functions of different coordinates, they must both be a constant, say some LLL. This gives :

LR=2r2R(V−E)−ddrr2ddrRLYsin⁡2α=sin⁡α∂∂αsin⁡α∂∂αY+∂2∂β2YLR = 2r^2R(V-E) - \frac{d}{dr}r^2 \frac{d}{dr}R \\ LY\sin^2\alpha = \sin\alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \sin\alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} Y + \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta^2}Y LR=2r2R(V−E)−drd​r2drd​RLYsin2α=sinα∂α∂​sinα∂α∂​Y+∂β2∂2​Y

Now, as we have arbitrary scaling for each part, we can WLOG assume that the angular part is normalised. Essentially, we require :

∫r=−∞∞∫α∫βR(r)2Y2(α,β)r2sin⁡αdrdαdβ=1  ⟹  [∫−∞∞R2(r)r2dr][∫α∫βY2(α,β)sin⁡αdαdβ]=1\int_{r=-\infty}^\infty\int_\alpha\int_\beta R(r)^2Y^2(\alpha,\beta) r^2\sin\alpha dr d\alpha d\beta = 1 \\\implies [\int_{-\infty}^\infty R^2(r)r^2 dr][\int_{\alpha}\int_\beta Y^2(\alpha,\beta) \sin\alpha d\alpha d\beta] =1 ∫r=−∞∞​∫α​∫β​R(r)2Y2(α,β)r2sinαdrdαdβ=1⟹[∫−∞∞​R2(r)r2dr][∫α​∫β​Y2(α,β)sinαdαdβ]=1

By ensuring that

∫α∫βY2(α,β)sin⁡αdαdβ=1\int_{\alpha}\int_\beta Y^2(\alpha,\beta) \sin\alpha d\alpha d\beta =1 ∫α​∫β​Y2(α,β)sinαdαdβ=1

we can then have the normalisation

∫−∞∞R2(r)r2dr=1\int_{-\infty}^\infty R^2(r)r^2 dr =1 ∫−∞∞​R2(r)r2dr=1

We can, in fact solve for YYY entirely without knowing what VVV is. The solution has basis functions of form Ym,lY_{m,l}Ym,l​ where m,lm,lm,l are integers. These are called the the azimuthal quantum number and the angular momentum quantum number. This derivation is carried out in detail in my Notes. But since we are only interested in the radial part, the only thing that we take from the results of that derivation is L−l(l+1)L - l(l+1)L−l(l+1).

Now, substituting L=−l(l+1)L = -l(l+1)L=−l(l+1) back into the equation for RRR, we get :

−l(l+1)R=2r2R(V−E)−ddrr2ddrR-l(l+1)R = 2r^2R(V-E) - \frac{d}{dr}r^2 \frac{d}{dr}R −l(l+1)R=2r2R(V−E)−drd​r2drd​R

Define u(r)=rR(r)  ⟹  R=u/ru(r)=rR(r) \implies R = u/ru(r)=rR(r)⟹R=u/r, giving us :

−l(l+1)ur=2ru(V−E)−ddr(ru′−u)  ⟹  −l(l+1)u=2r2u(V−E)−r(ru′′+u′−u′)  ⟹  u′′(r)=(2(V(r)−E)+l(l+1)r2) u(r)-l(l+1)\frac{u}{r} = 2ru(V-E) - \frac{d}{dr} (ru' -u) \\\implies -l(l+1)u = 2r^2u(V-E) - r (ru'' + u' - u') \\\implies \boxed{u''(r) = (2(V(r)-E) +\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}) \,u(r)} −l(l+1)ru​=2ru(V−E)−drd​(ru′−u)⟹−l(l+1)u=2r2u(V−E)−r(ru′′+u′−u′)⟹u′′(r)=(2(V(r)−E)+r2l(l+1)​)u(r)​

This is accompanied by the normalisation condition

∫−∞∞u2(r)dr=1\int_{-\infty}^\infty u^2(r)dr = 1 ∫−∞∞​u2(r)dr=1

and the expectation equation (assuming normalisation is done) :

⟨g(r)⟩=∫−∞∞g(r)u2(r)dr\braket{g(r)} = \int_{-\infty}^\infty g(r)u^2(r)dr ⟨g(r)⟩=∫−∞∞​g(r)u2(r)dr

Now, consider the a-dimensionalised electrostratic potential for an electron in some shell of a hydrogen atom, i.e. V(r)=−1/rV(r) = -1/rV(r)=−1/r. Plugging that in, we get :

u′′(r)=(−2E−2r+l(l+1)r2)u(r)  ⟺  −12d2dr2u(r)+[l(l+1)2r2−1r]u(r)=Eu(r)u''(r) = (-2E - \frac{2}{r} + \frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}) u(r) \iff\\ \boxed{-\frac{1}{2} \frac{d^2}{dr^2} u(r) + [\frac{l(l+1)}{2r^2} - \frac{1}{r}]u(r) = Eu(r)} u′′(r)=(−2E−r2​+r2l(l+1)​)u(r)⟺−21​dr2d2​u(r)+[2r2l(l+1)​−r1​]u(r)=Eu(r)​

The boxed equation is what the assignment refers to as the "radial equation" (though it's using u=rRu = rRu=rR and not RRR).

Define

Veff(r)=V(r)+l(l+1)2r2V_\text{eff}(r) = V(r) + \frac{l(l+1)}{2r^2} Veff​(r)=V(r)+2r2l(l+1)​

This can be interpreted as the potential in a rotating reference frame with angular momentum of l(l+1)\sqrt{l(l+1)}l(l+1)​. We had the same thing during planetary motion.

For the electrostatic potential of hydrogen, we have :

Veff(r)=−1r+l(l+1)2r2V_\text{eff}(r) = -\frac{1}{r} + \frac{l(l+1)}{2r^2} Veff​(r)=−r1​+2r2l(l+1)​

This function is plotted for several different values of lll in the figure.

Using this, we can rewrite the equation as :

u′′(r)=2(V(r)−E)u(r)  ⟺  −12d2dr2u(r)+Veffu(r)=Eu(r)u''(r) = 2(V(r)-E) u(r) \iff \\ -\frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2}{dr^2} u(r) + V_\text{eff} u(r) = E u(r) u′′(r)=2(V(r)−E)u(r)⟺−21​dr2d2​u(r)+Veff​u(r)=Eu(r)

This is similar to the usual TISE formulation, although u(r)u(r)u(r) is not really the wave function we want to finally be solving for. And again, similar to planetary motion, we can have bound states if E<VeffE < V_\text{eff}E<Veff​, meaning that the particle that the wavefunction represents is (classically) trapped in a potential well. However, note that the shape of the wavefunction (given by ∣ψ∣2|\psi|^2∣ψ∣2) doesn't change at all with time. The condition that E<VeffE < V_\text{eff}E<Veff​ is for the equation to have a physical solution.

Since the assignment asks to modify the potential in one of the parts, let us consider a more general potential of

V(r)=−Ze−μrr+λr2  ⟹  Veff(r)=−Ze−μrr+λr2+l(l+1)2r2V(r) = -\frac{Ze^{-\mu r}}{r} + \lambda r^2 \\\implies V_\text{eff}(r) = -\frac{Ze^{-\mu r}}{r} + \lambda r^2 + \frac{l(l+1)}{2r^2} V(r)=−rZe−μr​+λr2⟹Veff​(r)=−rZe−μr​+λr2+2r2l(l+1)​

This is what we will use for the implementation. Namely, we will have the function:

def electrostatic_potential_eff(r:(np.ndarray|float), l=0, mu=0, lamb=0, Z=1):
    return (lamb*r*r) + (l*(l+1)/(2*r*r)) - (Z*np.exp(-mu*r)/r)

Part (b),(c),(d) : Shooting method and Bound-State Energies

Theory and design

In general, the (1D) ATISE has 2 mathematical basis solutions for any E<0E < 0E<0; one physical (like we saw) and other non-physical which grows exponentially on the tails.

Define xm=12(xr+xl)x_m = \frac{1}{2}(x_r + x_l)xm​=21​(xr​+xl​). Then, one can get a mathematically unique solution for [xm,∞)[x_m, \infty)[xm​,∞) by setting uE(xr)=0u_E(x_r)=0uE​(xr​)=0 and uE′(xr)=vru_E'(x_r)=v_ruE′​(xr​)=vr​. This will be a linear combination of the physical solution that decays to 0 as x→∞x\to \inftyx→∞ and the non-phyiscal solution that explodes ∞\infty∞ instead. Now, by setting vrv_rvr​ as a very small value, the coefficient for the non-physical solution will be small (assuming xrx_rxr​ is large enough) and thus the contribution of the non-physical solution at xmx_mxm​ will be small. This means, that we will effectively recover the value of the physical solution as xmx_mxm​. The same goes for the derivative uE′u_E'uE′​ too (the non-physical solution's contribution to the derivative will be small at xmx_mxm​). Similarly, if we solve for (−∞,xm](-\infty, x_m](−∞,xm​], with uE(xl)=0u_E(x_l)=0uE​(xl​)=0 and uE′(xl)=vlu_E'(x_l)=v_luE′​(xl​)=vl​, the non-physical solution (which explodes to ±∞\pm \infty±∞ as x→∞x\to \inftyx→∞) will have very small contributions at xmx_mxm​ .

Furthermore, the exact values of vlv_lvl​ and vrv_rvr​ only scale the (non-normalised) solutions uE↑,uE↓u_E ^\uparrow, u_E^\downarrowuE↑​,uE↓​ for (−∞,xm](-\infty, x_m](−∞,xm​] and [xm,∞)[x_m, \infty)[xm​,∞) respectively. We know that for the correct values of vrv_rvr​ and vlv_lvl​, the physical solutions for the two halfs will become identical. Again, since this is a 2nd order ODE, this is equivalent to saying

uE↑(xm)=uE↓(xm)uE′↑(xm)=uE′↓(xm)u_E^\uparrow(x_m) = u_E^\downarrow(x_m) \\ u_E'^\uparrow(x_m) = u_E'^\downarrow(x_m) uE↑​(xm​)=uE↓​(xm​)uE′↑​(xm​)=uE′↓​(xm​)

But even without the correct ratio of vr,vlv_r, v_lvr​,vl​, what we do have is :

∃ C∈R   s.t.uE↑(xm)=CuE↓(xm)anduE′↑(xm)=CuE′↓(xm)  ⟹  f(E):=uE↑(xm)uE′↓(xm)−uE↓(xm)uE′↑(xm)=0\exist\, C \in \mathbb{R} \;\text{ s.t.} \quad u_E^\uparrow(x_m) = C u_E^\downarrow(x_m) \quad \text{and} \quad u_E'^\uparrow(x_m) = C u_E'^\downarrow(x_m) \\\implies f(E) := u_E^\uparrow(x_m) u_E'^\downarrow(x_m) - u_E^\downarrow(x_m)u_E'^\uparrow(x_m) = 0 ∃C∈R s.t.uE↑​(xm​)=CuE↓​(xm​)anduE′↑​(xm​)=CuE′↓​(xm​)⟹f(E):=uE↑​(xm​)uE′↓​(xm​)−uE↓​(xm​)uE′↑​(xm​)=0

Of course, for an EEE that is not an eigen-energy, we will have f(E)≠0f(E)\ne 0f(E)=0. As it turns out, this matching loss f(E)f(E)f(E) is actually the Wronskian of the two solutions (uE↑,uE↓u_E^\uparrow, u_E^\downarrowuE↑​,uE↓​). This is exactly 0, only when the two solutions (after normalisation) are the same (save for a sign change). Moreover it is not dependent on the matching point (which is the mid-point xmx_mxm​ in our case).

This is the basis for the shooting method. We choose extreme xl,xrx_l, x_rxl​,xr​ values (as per the spatial scale of the problem) and discretise the [xl,xm][x_l, x_m][xl​,xm​] and [xm,xr][x_m, x_r][xm​,xr​] segments. We set the boundary conditions for xl,xrx_l, x_rxl​,xr​ as described, with arbitrary, but small values of vl,vrv_l, v_rvl​,vr​ and solve the 2nd order ODE, for a given energy E<0E<0E<0 for the [xl,xm][x_l, x_m][xl​,xm​] segment and [xm,xr][x_m, x_r][xm​,xr​] segment individually (with the 2nd segment solved backwards from xrx_rxr​ to xmx_mxm​) to get the value of uE↑(xm),uE′↓(xm),uE↓(xm),uE′↑(xm)u_E^\uparrow(x_m),u_E'^\downarrow(x_m),u_E^\downarrow(x_m),u_E'^\uparrow(x_m)uE↑​(xm​),uE′↓​(xm​),uE↓​(xm​),uE′↑​(xm​) and thus f(E)f(E)f(E). Solving the 2nd order ODE can be done using any method, say RK2; but since the integration often passes through a region containing the "classical turning (inflection) point" and can be over-whelmed by (auto-regressive) noise due to numerical errors, an integrator with superior accuracy (such as Numerov's method) is preffered. The goal is to verify whether EEE is an eigen-energy by checking whether f(E)≈0f(E)\approx 0f(E)≈0.

Although, we can zero-in on a particular eigen-energy using bisection methods in log⁡2(NE)\log_2(N_E)log2​(NE​) time were NEN_ENE​ is the number of values of EEE (regularly spaced) that we will test. I instead want to create plots for f(E)f(E)f(E) itself. To do this, I will define:

u⃗(x)=[uEk(x)]kv⃗(x)=[uEk′(x)]kE⃗=[Ek]k\vec u(x) = [u_{E_k}(x)]_k \\ \vec v(x) = [u'_{E_k}(x)]_k \\ \vec E = [E_k]_k u(x)=[uEk​​(x)]k​v(x)=[uEk​′​(x)]k​E=[Ek​]k​

and re-write the ATISE as :

ddxv⃗(x)=2(V(x)−E⃗)∗u⃗(x)=K(x)⃗∗u⃗(x)=a⃗(x)ddxu⃗(x)=v(x)\frac{d}{dx} \vec v(x) = 2(V(x)-\vec E)* \vec u(x) = \vec{K(x)}*\vec u(x) = \vec a(x)\\ \frac{d}{dx} \vec u(x) = v(x) dxd​v(x)=2(V(x)−E)∗u(x)=K(x)​∗u(x)=a(x)dxd​u(x)=v(x)

Here, the "∗*∗" symbol represents point-wise multiplication.

Now, it's worth noting that since we cannot integrate over r=0r=0r=0 (since there is a singularity for VeffV_\text{eff}Veff​), our interval [rl,rr][r_l, r_r][rl​,rr​] must lie in the r>0r>0r>0 region entirely. This is different from the assumptions we made while developing the Shooting method. In particular, we assumed that xl,xrx_l, x_rxl​,xr​ are extreme values, for which the physical solution will have small value and derivative, while the non-physical solution will have values with large magnitudes. Here, though rlr_lrl​ is not extreme, it still has the property we need, namely that the physical solution for u(r)=rR(r)u(r)=rR(r)u(r)=rR(r) will have a small value (though R(r)R(r)R(r) may not have small values) and the non-physical solution, which has the asymptotics of r−lr^{-l}r−l will have a large values.

Results

In the right-side of the figure, you can see the plots for f(E)f(E)f(E) for different values of lll. Using these, the eigen-energies were identified. For these eigen-energies (and corresponding values of lll), the eigen-states were computed by numerically solving the radial wave equation in u(r)u(r)u(r). These are plotted to the left side in the figure. The corresponding energies are shown in the figure too. For each energy, the principal quantum number nnn (in the subscript; e.g. E2E_2E2​) was computed using this function :

def E2n(E):return int(round((-2*E)**-0.5))

This is because the energy is given by En=−12n2E_n = -\frac{1}{2n^2}En​=−2n21​. The exact values numerically computed for different sub-shells are :

  • 1s: -0.4999985 = -12×12\frac{1}{2\times 1^2}2×121​ + 1.4894565203982246e-06
  • 2s: -0.1249965 = -12×22\frac{1}{2\times 2^2}2×221​ + 3.467043051791352e-06
  • 3s: -0.0555466 = -12×32\frac{1}{2\times 3^2}2×321​ + 8.960942531388572e-06
  • 2p: -0.1249962 = -12×22\frac{1}{2\times 2^2}2×221​ + 3.781354790802216e-06
  • 3p: -0.0555462 = -12×32\frac{1}{2\times 3^2}2×321​ + 9.34720833578595e-06
  • 3d: -0.0555472 = -12×32\frac{1}{2\times 3^2}2×321​ + 8.389867257103945e-06

This gives the transition energy from the n=2n=2n=2 shell to n=1n=1n=1 as around 0.375001978 in atomic units, which is close to the theoretical value of 0.375. Mutiplying by E0≈27.2eVE_0 \approx 27.2 \text{eV}E0​≈27.2eV, this corresponds to around 10.20005eV10.20005 \text{eV}10.20005eV, which is close to the theoretical value of the first Lyman transition energy, i.e. 10.2eV10.2 \text{eV}10.2eV.

From the figure, you can also manually count the number of nodes for each eigenstate as the number of times that curve for u(r)u(r)u(r) cuts the x-axis (except at r=0r=0r=0). As you can easily verify from the plots, this number is always exactly n−l−1n-l-1n−l−1. For example in the top-left subplot (for the l=0l=0l=0 case, i.e. s orbitals), when n=1n=1n=1 (blue curve), we have no points (other than r=0r=0r=0) where the curve crosses the x-axis. For n=2n=2n=2 (2s orbital, orange curve), it happens once, very roughly at r≈2r\approx 2r≈2. For n=3n=3n=3, it happens twice, first around 2 and then around 7. Similarly for the l=1l=1l=1 case, the n=3n=3n=3 curve (orange) cuts the x-axis n−l−1=1n-l-1 = 1n−l−1=1 times (around r=6r=6r=6) and the n=2n=2n=2 curve doesn't cut. Notice that there is no curve for n=1n=1n=1, since we don't have a physical solution for the resultant E−VeffE-V_\text{eff}E−Veff​.

You can also notice that the energies for the 3s (E3, l=0E_3,\, l=0E3​,l=0),3p (E3, l=1E_3,\, l=1E3​,l=1), and 3d (E3, l=2E_3,\, l=2E3​,l=2) states are all the same (−0.055ˉ-0.05\bar 5−0.055ˉ). Similarly, those for 2s and 2p states are the same (-0.125). Thus, there is a degeneracy in the energy levels, i.e. for the same eigen-energy, you can have multiple values of lll.

Part (f): Degeneracy Breaking

Since En=−12n2E_n = -\frac{1}{2n^2}En​=−2n21​, thus the different VeffV_\text{eff}Veff​ functions for different lll values, all give us the same energy levels. This is something that only happens for the Coulumbic potential V(r)=−Z/rV(r)=-Z/rV(r)=−Z/r. To demonstrate this fact, we will use the generalised modified-effective-potential mentioned earlier and numerically solve for the eigen-energies using the shooting method for cases where μ≠0\mu\ne 0μ=0 or λ≠0\lambda\ne 0λ=0. The resultant plots for f(E)f(E)f(E) and eigenstates are shown in the figure. To ensure each energy level can be mapped to an energy level for the unmodified case, but we can still notice loss in degeneracy, I have chosed μ=10−2\mu=10^{-2}μ=10−2 and λ=10−5\lambda=10^{-5}λ=10−5 for this analysis.

For a more accurate analysis, the differences in the energy levels closest to 2s and 2p states (for the l=0l=0l=0 and l=1l=1l=1 case) were computed. These were the results :

  • Normal : ∣E2s−E2p∣≈3.14×10−7|E_{2s} - E_{2p}| \approx 3.14\times 10^{-7}∣E2s​−E2p​∣≈3.14×10−7
  • λ\lambdaλ = 1e-05 : ∣E2s−E2p∣≈1.18×10−4|E_{2s} - E_{2p}| \approx 1.18\times 10^{-4}∣E2s​−E2p​∣≈1.18×10−4
  • μ\muμ = 0.01$ : ∣E2s−E2p∣≈4.94×10−5|E_{2s} - E_{2p}| \approx 4.94\times 10^{-5}∣E2s​−E2p​∣≈4.94×10−5

As you can see, there is significantly more difference between the energy levels of these states when the potential is modified. This is even clearer when n=3n=3n=3 is considered (see figure for the energy values). The little bit of difference between the energy states fir the un-modified potential is due to small numerical errors and can be considered noise.

Project 3: 2D Quantum Scattering

Part (a) : Numerical method

We can extend the split operator method to 2D by assuming Δy=Δx\Delta y = \Delta xΔy=Δx and defining

a(x,y)=4mΔx2tℏi−2mΔx2ℏ2V(x,y)−4b(x,y)=4mΔx2tℏi+2mΔx2ℏ2V(x,y)+4a(x,y) = \frac{4m\Delta x^2}{t\hbar}i - \frac{2m\Delta x^2}{\hbar^2}V(x,y) -4 \\ b(x,y) = \frac{4m\Delta x^2}{t\hbar}i + \frac{2m\Delta x^2}{\hbar^2}V(x,y) + 4 a(x,y)=tℏ4mΔx2​i−ℏ22mΔx2​V(x,y)−4b(x,y)=tℏ4mΔx2​i+ℏ22mΔx2​V(x,y)+4

and writing

[0101a(x)1010]∘[ψt(x+Δx,y+Δy)ψt(x,y+Δy)ψt(x−Δx,y+Δy)ψt(x+Δx,y)ψt(x,y)ψt(x−Δx,y)ψt(x+Δx,y−Δy)ψt(x,y−Δy)ψt(x−Δx,y−Δy)]=[0−10−1b(x)−10−10]∘[ψ0(x+Δx,y+Δy)ψ0(x,y+Δy)ψ0(x−Δx,y+Δy)ψ0(x+Δx,y)ψ0(x,y)ψ0(x−Δx,y)ψ0(x+Δx,y−Δy)ψ0(x,y−Δy)ψ0(x−Δx,y−Δy)]\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & a(x) & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \circ \begin{bmatrix} \psi_t(x+\Delta x,y+\Delta y) & \psi_t(x,y+\Delta y) & \psi_t(x-\Delta x,y+\Delta y) \\ \psi_t(x+\Delta x,y) & \psi_t(x,y) & \psi_t(x-\Delta x,y) \\ \psi_t(x+\Delta x,y-\Delta y) & \psi_t(x,y-\Delta y) & \psi_t(x-\Delta x,y-\Delta y) \\ \end{bmatrix} \\ = \\ \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & b(x) & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \circ \begin{bmatrix} \psi_0(x+\Delta x,y+\Delta y) & \psi_0(x,y+\Delta y) & \psi_0(x-\Delta x,y+\Delta y) \\ \psi_0(x+\Delta x,y) & \psi_0(x,y) & \psi_0(x-\Delta x,y) \\ \psi_0(x+\Delta x,y-\Delta y) & \psi_0(x,y-\Delta y) & \psi_0(x-\Delta x,y-\Delta y) \\ \end{bmatrix} ​010​1a(x)1​010​​∘​ψt​(x+Δx,y+Δy)ψt​(x+Δx,y)ψt​(x+Δx,y−Δy)​ψt​(x,y+Δy)ψt​(x,y)ψt​(x,y−Δy)​ψt​(x−Δx,y+Δy)ψt​(x−Δx,y)ψt​(x−Δx,y−Δy)​​=​0−10​−1b(x)−1​0−10​​∘​ψ0​(x+Δx,y+Δy)ψ0​(x+Δx,y)ψ0​(x+Δx,y−Δy)​ψ0​(x,y+Δy)ψ0​(x,y)ψ0​(x,y−Δy)​ψ0​(x−Δx,y+Δy)ψ0​(x−Δx,y)ψ0​(x−Δx,y−Δy)​​

Solving this is going to be a nightmare.

So instead, we approximate even more, giving us what is known as the Alternat Direction Implicit method.

Here, we split the hamiltonian operator as H^=H^x+H^y\hat H = \hat H_x + \hat H_yH^=H^x​+H^y​ where

H^x=−ℏ2p^x22m+Vx(x,y)H^y=−ℏ2p^y22m+Vy(x,y)\hat H_x = -\frac{\hbar^2 \hat p_x^2}{2m} + V_x(x,y) \\ \hat H_y = -\frac{\hbar^2 \hat p_y^2}{2m} + V_y(x,y) H^x​=−2mℏ2p^​x2​​+Vx​(x,y)H^y​=−2mℏ2p^​y2​​+Vy​(x,y)

It it's possible to separate the potential as V(x,y)=Vx(x)+Vy(y)V(x,y) = V_x(x) + V_y(y)V(x,y)=Vx​(x)+Vy​(y), we can simply split it. Otherwise, we can do Vx=Vy=V/2V_x = V_y = V/2Vx​=Vy​=V/2

Now, for the method, we discretise the wave-function over a grid, giving us the matrix Ψ[y,x]\Psi[y,x]Ψ[y,x]. Just like before, we create the tri-diagonal matrices (using t/2t/2t/2 rather than ttt), but now for each dimension separately. Then we solve :

Ax(y)Ψt/2[y]=Bx(y)Ψ0[y]A_{x}(y)\Psi_{t/2}[y] = B_x(y)\Psi_0[y] Ax​(y)Ψt/2​[y]=Bx​(y)Ψ0​[y]

for all yyy and then

Ay(x)ΨtT[x]=By(x)Ψt/2T[x]A_y(x)\Psi_{t}^T[x] = B_y(x)\Psi_{t/2}^T[x] Ay​(x)ΨtT​[x]=By​(x)Ψt/2T​[x]

for all xxx.

This effectively takes O(MN)O(MN)O(MN) operations each iteration, assuming the grid is M×NM\times NM×N points big.

Note that this analysis was done for the physical 2D TDSE, which is :

−ℏ22m∇2ψ+Vψ=iℏ∂∂tψ-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2 \psi + V \psi = i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi −2mℏ2​∇2ψ+Vψ=iℏ∂t∂​ψ

The Ax(y)A_x(y)Ax​(y) and By(x)B_y(x)By​(x) need to be translated to the adimensional versions (as done in CQM.py) for implementation.

As suggested in the assignment, the grid will have x,y∈[−20,20]x,y \in [-20,20]x,y∈[−20,20] and Δy=Δx=0.1\Delta y = \Delta x = 0.1Δy=Δx=0.1. We will have Δt=0.003\Delta t = 0.003Δt=0.003 for all the animations created (and the respective plots).

Part (a): Boundary Conditions and Normalization

Similar to the 1D case, we use perfectly reflecting boundaries that have ψ=0\psi=0ψ=0 at all times. For normalisation, we will ensure that

Nx⃗(t)=⟨ψt∣ψt⟩≈Δx2∑x∑yψt[x,y]=1+ϵtN_{\vec x}(t) = \braket{\psi_t | \psi_t} \approx \Delta x^2\sum_x\sum_y \psi_t[x,y] = 1 + \epsilon_t Nx​(t)=⟨ψt​∣ψt​⟩≈Δx2x∑​y∑​ψt​[x,y]=1+ϵt​

where ϵt\epsilon_tϵt​, the error, is a small quantity, arising from rounding and discretization errors. Just like before, we will plot Nx⃗(t)N_{\vec x}(t)Nx​(t) as a function of time/step. We will also compute the 2D FFT of ψt\psi_tψt​, giving the momentum wave-function ϕt\phi_tϕt​ and its norm Np⃗(t)=⟨ϕt∣ϕt⟩N_{\vec p}(t) = \braket{\phi_t| \phi_t}Np​​(t)=⟨ϕt​∣ϕt​⟩.

As suggested in the assignment, the wave-packet will be centered at (−8,0)(-8,0)(−8,0) and have an initial momentum kxk_xkx​ to the right (with ky=0k_y=0ky​=0). The wave-packet will be gaussian and have the spread of σ=1\sigma=1σ=1 in either direction, which is much smaller than the grid's dimensions and will prevent the boundary affecting the simulation.

Part (b): Free Propagation

Once again, as you can see, towards the end of the simulation, the momentum in xxx directon starts to change (invert, more specifically). This is due to the reflection of the wave-packet by the right boundary of the grid.

Also notice how the norm ⟨ψ∣ψ⟩\braket{\psi|\psi}⟨ψ∣ψ⟩ stays close to 1, with variation being on the order of 10−1210^{-12}10−12

Part (c) and (f): Repulsive Barrier and classical shadow region

You can see in the animation that after the wave-packet encounters the repulsive disk potential, there is a wavefront (a little after the first thin reflection) travelling to the left. This is the reflected wave. Notice that there is some of the incident probability mass that actually goes inside and beyond the disk, i.e. in the region where x>R=3x>R=3x>R=3 and y∈[−R/2,R/2]=[−1.5,1.5]y\in [-R/2,R/2] = [-1.5, 1.5]y∈[−R/2,R/2]=[−1.5,1.5]. This is the classical "shadow region". No classical particle with momentum purely along x-axis would ever be able to reach the shadow region. And of course, classically, no particle will be able to enter the disk. But here we see that a quantum particle/wave (or something close to a particle) is able to enter the disk and go beyond it into the shadow region. In wave-mechanics terms, this is the transmitted wave, and is a very standard phenomenon to see.

You can also see (in the animation) the most probable and mean positions overlayed on the heat-map for ∣ψ∣2|\psi|^2∣ψ∣2 as well as the most probable and mean momentums overlayed on the heat-map for the squared magnitude of the momentum wavefunction, i.e. ∣ϕ∣2(k⃗)|\phi|^2(\vec k)∣ϕ∣2(k).

Notice how the mean momentum barely shifts and how the momentum wavefunction, at one point, has a hole in the place where the mean momentum is, indicating scattering of the particle into many different directions.

Part (e): Angular Distribution

The assignment asks to compute P(θ)=∫∣ψ(r,θ)∣2rdrP(\theta) = \int |\psi(r,\theta)|^2 r drP(θ)=∫∣ψ(r,θ)∣2rdr "far from the scatterer" and to "interpret it as a numerical cross section". This part was confusing for these reasons :

  1. The integral isn't an area integral, but rather a line integral.
  2. If the interval over which we are integrating is too small, we will get significant values only when the particle is passing through the region, which will not be sufficient to understand the physics of scattering.

So, I have made a few modifications :

  1. I consider wide sectors (centered at given θm\theta_mθm​) with angular width of Δθ=10o=π18\Delta \theta = 10^o = \frac{\pi}{18}Δθ=10o=18π​ which are then further cropped so that r∈[rm−Δr,rm+Δr]r\in [r_m-\Delta r, r_m + \Delta r]r∈[rm​−Δr,rm​+Δr] where Δr\Delta rΔr is a large value. I then compute the area integral of ∣ψ∣2|\psi|^2∣ψ∣2 over these regions giving P(θm∣rm,Δr,Δθ)P(\theta_m|r_m, \Delta r, \Delta \theta)P(θm​∣rm​,Δr,Δθ)
  2. To make sure a good amount of the probability mass is captured, I have kept rm=13r_m=13rm​=13 and Δr=7\Delta r = 7Δr=7 (in atomic units).

For this section, refer back to the animation in part (c). These rm−Δrr_m-\Delta rrm​−Δr and rm+Δrr_m + \Delta rrm​+Δr values are highlighted as white concentric circles in the first subplot of the animation. The resultant values of P(θm)P(\theta_m)P(θm​) are plotted on the radial plot in bottom right subplot of the animation, with a square root taken to somewhat compress the dynamic range and help in visualisation.

Part (d): Parameter Variations

R=1R=1R=1

With a smaller RRR, less of the probability mass is directly reflected back, and surprisingly, less probability mass is directly transmitted. Rather, it seems that wave is converted into 2 waves going travelling diagonally to the right, which then interfere when they spread. The shape of the P(θ)P(\theta)P(θ) plot after the encounter with the disk is also different, with the central peak we previously saw missing.

R=0.3R=0.3R=0.3

With an even smaller RRR, the shape of P(θ)P(\theta)P(θ) after the encounter with the disk entirely changes to a more circular shape. Moreover, there is little to no change in the momentum wave-function before and after the encounter. Most likely the two diagonally travelling wavefronts we saw in the R=1R=1R=1 case are spreading more rapidly and interfering earlier in the shadow region. Thus, the probability mass in the shadow region isn't due to the transmitted wave, but rather interference of the deflected wavefronts.

kx=5k_x=5kx​=5

The interesting thing to notice is that when kx=5k_x=5kx​=5, the particle entirely bypasses the repulsive disk. It is effectively going over the disk, because it has a much higher energy (around 13) than the potential of the disk (just 1).

Part (f): Attractive Potential

Unlike the repulsive potential where most of the probability mass is reflected back, for an attractive potential, most is transmitted through, although there is some that is reflected back. Similar to the decrease in momentum we saw when the particle entered the region with higher potential, here we see an increase in the average momentum. Just like last time, at the end of the simulation, we start seeing the effect of the reflective boundary.

Part (g): Convergence Tests

From the figure, we can gather than even after increaseing Δt\Delta tΔt to 0.1 and increasing Δx\Delta xΔx to 0.2, the numerical solution is accurate.

Only when we increase Δ\DeltaΔ to 0.5 do we start getting inaccuracies. Even then, the general shape of the solution is the same.
